title: Choose SQL vs NoSQL for a high write workload
description: Decide between PostgreSQL and Cassandra for an event ingestion pipeline processing 50,000 writes per second with strict latency requirements.

data.text: Your analytics platform needs to ingest 50,000 user events per second from 200K concurrent mobile clients. Queries must return results within 200ms. The events are append-only and immutable once written. Your team knows PostgreSQL extremely well. Do you use it, or do you reach for Cassandra?

terms.definition: A distributed system can guarantee at most two of: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the guarantees provided by traditional relational databases.
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency: the typical NoSQL availability model.
The sequence of components an event passes through from client to persistent storage.
The system continues operating despite arbitrary message loss or delay between nodes.

data.title: CAP reality check
data.text: In the presence of network partitions (which will happen), you must choose between Consistency and Availability. No real-world system gives you both. PostgreSQL chooses CP; Cassandra chooses AP with tunable consistency.

cards.title: PostgreSQL
cards.description: ACID-compliant relational database with rich query capabilities.
pros: Strong consistency and ACID transactions out of the box
Rich query language with joins, aggregations, and window functions
Single-node write performance is extremely high with WAL optimization
Your team already knows it well
cons: Horizontal scaling requires Citus or sharding logic
Sustained 50K writes per second requires careful partitioning
Replication lag under heavy write load can break consistency assumptions
Adding nodes is not as seamless as Cassandra

cards.title: Cassandra
cards.description: Wide-column NoSQL store designed for linear scalability and high write throughput.
pros: Linear write scalability: add nodes, gain capacity
No single point of failure; masterless ring architecture
Tunable consistency: QUORUM reads and writes
cons: Eventual consistency means stale reads are possible
Compaction storms and tombstones require operational expertise

data.title: PostgreSQL: Relational event schema
data.content: Normalized schema with foreign keys and constraints.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       UUID NOT NULL,
  event_type    TEXT NOT NULL,
  payload       JSONB NOT NULL,
  occurred_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  received_at   TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
  device        TEXT
);

CREATE INDEX idx_events_user_time ON events (user_id, occurred_at);

-- Query with aggregation:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', occurred_at) AS hour,
       count(*) AS event_count
FROM events
WHERE user_id = $1
GROUP BY hour
ORDER BY hour DESC
LIMIT 24;

data.title: Cassandra: Partitioned, denormalized table
data.content: Primary key designed for time-range queries on a partition.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE events (
  user_id    UUID,
  occurred_at TIMESTAMP,
  event_type TEXT,
  payload    BLOB,
  device     TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, occurred_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (occurred_at DESC);

-- Query all events for a user:
SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = ? LIMIT 100;

-- No joins. If you need event_type counts, pre-aggregate into a summary table.

data.caption: CAP theorem: choose two, sacrifice one
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[CAP Theorem] --> B[Consistency]
    A --> C[Availability]
    A --> D[Partition Tolerance]
    B -->|Must choose| E[One of C or A]
    C -->|Must choose| E
    D -->|Always required in distributed systems| F[Network failures happen]
    E --> G[SQL: Consistency + Partition Tolerance]
    E --> H[NoSQL: Availability + Partition Tolerance]

items.text: Can you tolerate eventual consistency for read-after-write scenarios?
Is your query pattern fixed, or do you need ad-hoc analytics?
Do you have operational expertise to manage a Cassandra ring?
Will write volume grow beyond a single PostgreSQL node's IOPS ceiling?
Are your access patterns predictable enough for denormalization?

data.title: Recommended approach: PostgreSQL with Citus for this workload
data.content: 50K writes per second is achievable on PostgreSQL with proper partitioning, connection pooling, and WAL tuning. Your team's existing expertise reduces operational risk. If you later need to scale reads, add read replicas. If writes outgrow a single node, Citus distributes the table without requiring a data model rewrite.

data.title: When to choose Cassandra instead
data.text: Cassandra is the right choice when writes exceed 200K per second, your access patterns are strictly time-series and never require ad-hoc joins, and you have dedicated SRE expertise. For 50K writes with complex query needs, PostgreSQL is the safer bet.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: CAP is not a menu: network partitions happen, so you choose between CP and AP.
PostgreSQL with Citus or read replicas handles most 'high write' workloads.
Cassandra's complexity is justified only at massive scale with a dedicated team.
data.takeaway: Choose the database your team can operate correctly under pressure.
